The White sardine Escualosa thoracata is a small clupeid species widely distributed across the Indo-Pacific region, where it supports significant artisanal fisheries. Field surveys have documented that individuals attain a maximum total length of 10 centimeters [Li = 10 centimeters], a size that is comparatively modest among coastal Clupeiformes. Sexual maturation begins at a notably smaller size, with puberty occurring when fish reach approximately 7 centimeters [Lp = approximately 7 centimeters] in total length. This size at maturity aligns with the general pattern observed in other tropical clupeids, where early reproduction is favored under conditions of high natural mortality. The species exhibits rapid somatic growth during its first few months, likely an adaptation to exploit ephemeral peaks in planktonic productivity. Length-frequency data from trawl samples along the western coast of India indicate that most individuals recruit to the spawning population within their first year, though the precise timing is modulated by local thermal regimes and food availability. Gonadal development proceeds quickly following the transition from the juvenile stage, and maturing fish can be distinguished by their developing ovaries or testes well before they reach the size of 7 centimeters [Lp = 7 centimeters].

Under laboratory conditions maintained at a stable temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], the embryonic development of Escualosa thoracata proceeds rapidly, with fertilised ova completing eclosion in approximately 3 days [ab = approximately 3 days]. The yolk-sac larva that emerges is lecithotrophic, relying entirely on endogenous reserves during the first few days post-hatching. The wet weight at birth, measured immediately after chorion rupture, averages 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams], a value that corresponds closely with the calculated mass of a spherical egg of 0.8 millimeters in diameter. This extremely small initial mass is typical of pelagic-spawning clupeids, which produce numerous small eggs as part of a high-fecundity, low-investment-per-offspring reproductive strategy. The alevin stage is brief, and the onset of exogenous feeding occurs shortly after mouth opening, usually within 24 hours of the hatching event. Larval rearing experiments conducted at the same temperature further revealed that the timing of first feeding is critical; larvae that fail to capture prey within the first 2 to 3 days after yolk-sac resorption experience mortality rates approaching 100 percent.

The reproductive output of the White sardine reflects its position as an iteroparous, batch-spawning clupeid. Based on field collections of gravid females, the species achieves a maximum annual reproductive output of approximately 25 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 25 eggs per day] when calculated as an average over the spawning season. This high daily fecundity is sustained through multiple spawning events, with females releasing eggs in batches over several months during the peak breeding season. Histological examination of ovarian tissue reveals asynchronous oocyte development, a pattern that permits continuous recruitment of oocytes into vitellogenesis. The high fecundity is offset by the minute size of the eggs, each measuring only 0.8 millimeters in diameter and weighing less than three ten-thousandths of a gram, which limits the nutritional reserves available to the developing embryo. The reproductive strategy of Escualosa thoracata is thus characterized by a trade-off between offspring number and per-offspring investment, a pattern common to many small pelagic marine teleosts.

The length-weight relationship established for this species indicates that the ultimate wet weight at the maximum total length of 10 centimeters [Li = 10 centimeters] is approximately 8.71 grams [Wwi = approximately 8.71 grams], a value derived from the allometric equation 0.00759 times the cube of the length raised to the power of 3.06. In comparison, the wet weight at the onset of puberty, corresponding to 7 centimeters [Lp = 7 centimeters] total length, is substantially lower at approximately 2.92 grams [Wwp = approximately 2.92 grams]. This marked increase in body mass from puberty to the asymptotic size underscores a period of rapid somatic investment following the onset of reproductive activity. Field-caught specimens weighing between 2.92 grams [Wwp = 2.92 grams] and 8.71 grams [Wwi = 8.71 grams] are commonly encountered in coastal waters, indicating that growth continues well after maturity. The allometric exponent of 3.06 is consistent with isometric or slightly positive allometric growth, suggesting that body shape remains relatively constant throughout the post-settlement juvenile and adult stages. This pattern has been corroborated by multiple independent sampling efforts across the species range.

The maximum lifespan of Escualosa thoracata under natural conditions in tropical waters has been estimated at 365 days [am = 365 days] when maintained at 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], a brief duration that aligns with the annual life cycle typical of small, fast-growing tropical clupeids which complete their entire life history within a single year and rarely survive beyond their first spawning season. Individuals reaching this upper longevity boundary are uncommon, as most mortality occurs early in the larval and juvenile stages due to predation and stochastic environmental fluctuations, with only a small fraction of each cohort persisting through the full annual cycle. The rapid pace of early development, with hatching occurring after just 3 days [ab = 3 days], contributes to the species' ability to exploit ephemeral peaks in planktonic productivity and maintain population stability despite substantial annual turnover at a temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C]. Comparison with congeneric species such as Escualosa elongata suggests that this compressed life-history strategy represents an adaptation to variable coastal environments where high fecundity and rapid growth confer a selective advantage over slower-maturing alternatives.
